st.headline: Man wrongly transfers $6,650 to ex-wife; ‘highly unreasonable’ conduct costs her over $7,000
st.teaser: She did not return the money despite his repeated requests, and later deposited it with the police instead.
fullText: SINGAPORE – Instead of transferring $6,650 to fintech platform Wise, James Jonathan accidentally sent the money to his ex-wife Adel Ng because he had saved her in his contact list as “Wife”.
What followed was a six-month legal dispute that involved a police report, an unsuccessful application to strike out the man’s claim and allegations of misconduct against his lawyers.
The ex-wife has now been ordered to pay $6,500 in legal costs after a magistrate’s court found that her conduct was “highly unreasonable” and that she had unnecessarily prolonged the dispute.
In a judgment released on Sept 7, Deputy Registrar Mark Lim said the case could have been resolved immediately after the mistaken transfer.
Instead, the $6,650 ended up with the police and in court.
The former couple had divorced in 2021 but remained in contact over matters, including access to their child.
After Jonathan mistakenly transferred the money to Ng on Dec 7, 2025, he sent her at least 10 e-mails between Dec 7 and Dec 15, asking her to return the money.
It was only after the man sent a letter of demand through his lawyers on Dec 17 that she responded through her lawyers.

But rather than simply returning the money, the woman on Dec 25 claimed that she was concerned that she was a victim of a possible scam and asked for extensive information, including the man’s identity number, a copy of an identity document, the source of the money, why the transfer had been made in error and why it was urgent that the money be returned.
She asked him to indemnify her against “any and all liabilities and expenses” arising from her returning the money.
The next day, Dec 26, Ng deposited the $6,650 with the Singapore Police Force.

In her police report, she said she wanted to return the money “under cover of this police report” to avoid any misunderstanding or involvement with money from a questionable source or “bad actors (e.g., scammers and money launderers)”.
She said she believed the police were the proper authority to determine whether the claim for the money was legitimate.
On Dec 30, Jonathan sued Ng to seek the return of the $6,650.

In her defence, the woman described herself as a “passive recipient” of money from an “unknown and unverifiable source” and said she believed there was a real possibility that she was receiving scam messages.
“Insofar as the defendant justifies her conduct by claiming that she was concerned that she was ‘confronted with a possible scam’, this beggars belief,” said the deputy registrar.

The two had previously corresponded by e-mail using the same addresses, the court noted. If she had any genuine concern about whether the e-mails were really from her former husband, nothing would have stopped her from checking with him directly.
“This is not a case of a complete stranger seeking the return of monies wrongly transferred,” said the deputy registrar.
The court also found that her requests for information on Dec 25 did not appear to be a genuine attempt to establish the man’s identity.
Rather, they appear calculated to vex her ex-husband, the deputy registrar said.
The requests were excessive, including demands for the source of the money, the reasons for the error, an identity document and wide indemnities.
More importantly, the woman did not appear to have genuinely been waiting for a response.
She made her police report and deposited the money with the police the very next day, without giving the man a reasonable opportunity to respond.
“It also bears noting that the request was made to the (ex-husband’s) solicitors on Christmas Day, when they could not reasonably have been expected to be working,” said the deputy registrar.
The dispute continued after the lawsuit was filed.

In May 2026, the woman applied to the court to strike out the man’s claim for the return of the money. The court described the application as “ill-conceived and without merit”, noting that she had failed to identify any specific ground for striking out the claim.
The deputy registrar said it appeared she had “retaliated” after the man filed his own application to strike out her defence.

She also made what the court described as “grave allegations” against the man and his lawyers, claiming that his lawyer had breached an undertaking to file a supplementary affidavit before a deadline and that the man had breached court directions to do the same.
The allegations prompted the court to call an in-person hearing at short notice, after which it found her allegations to be without merit.
The woman apologised “unreservedly” to the court and the man’s lawyer over the allegation concerning the solicitor.

cna.headline: JPMorgan names APAC, EMEA tech investment banking chiefs as international co-heads
cna.teaser: JPMorgan names APAC, EMEA tech investment banking chiefs as international co-heads
fullText: Sept 8 : JPMorgan Chase & Co has appointed its Asia Pacific and EMEA technology investment banking chiefs as co-heads of international technology investment banking, according to a memo issued by the company and seen by Reuters on Tuesday.

• Mark Fiteny, head of Asia-Pacific Technology, Media, and Telecom (APAC TMT) and New Economy Investment Banking, and Matt Gehl, head of EMEA Technology Investment Banking, were named co-heads of International Technology Investment Banking, the memo showed.
• The appointments were confirmed by a company spokesperson.

• The bank also named Pieter Himpe, currently head of EMEA Internet and Tech Services within its technology investment banking division, as co-head of EMEA Technology Investment Banking alongside veteran banker Bill Hutchings.
• Gehl will remain based in London and Fiteny in Hong Kong.

listening.title: Singapore's Hawker Centres Face Ingredient Cost Pressures
listening.transcript: As global food supply chains face ongoing disruptions, Singapore’s iconic hawker centres are feeling the pinch. Many stall owners are reluctant to pass the soaring costs of meat and vegetables directly onto budget-conscious patrons. To cope, some hawkers are tweaking their portions or absorbing the losses, hoping that inflation will soon taper off. Meanwhile, the government has announced new support measures to help these micro-businesses survive the challenging economic climate.

economistArticle.title: The Sticky Squeeze: Inflation's Stubborn Comeback
paras: The short-lived optimism that inflation had been permanently tamed has evaporated. Across major economies, consumer prices are ticking upward once more, driven by resilient consumer spending, volatile energy markets, and stubborn supply-chain bottlenecks. Central bankers, who had spent the previous quarters hinting at imminent interest-rate cuts, now find themselves forced to recalibrate their strategies.

The Federal Reserve and its global peers are grappling with a monetary policy dilemma. If they ease monetary conditions too quickly, they risk letting inflation expectations become deeply entrenched in the public consciousness. Conversely, keeping interest rates elevated for too long threatens to tip fragile economies into outright recession, suffocating business investment and hiring.

The geopolitical landscape further complicates this high-stakes balancing act. Shipping disruptions in key maritime corridors have pushed freight rates to levels unseen since the pandemic era, while geopolitical tensions in the Middle East cast a persistent shadow over global oil supplies. These supply-side shocks are largely immune to the blunt instrument of higher interest rates, leaving monetary authorities in a precarious position.

For open, trade-dependent economies like Singapore, these global crosscurrents are particularly acute. The Monetary Authority of Singapore must constantly calibrate its exchange-rate-based policy to shield domestic consumers from imported inflation without severely blunting export competitiveness. It is a delicate economic tightrope walk that leaves little room for policy missteps.

Ultimately, the return of inflation serves as a sobering reminder that the post-pandemic economic transition is far from complete. Structural shifts, including the costly green energy transition and the restructuring of global supply chains, suggest that the era of ultra-low inflation and rock-bottom interest rates may be gone for good. Businesses and consumers alike must brace for a prolonged period of macroeconomic volatility.
economistArticle.cn:
认为通胀已得到永久控制的短暂乐观情绪已经消散。受强劲的消费支出、波动不定的能源市场以及顽固的供应链瓶颈推动，各大主要经济体消费价格再度走高。在过去几个季度里一直暗示即将降息的各国央行，如今发现自己不得不重新调整其策略。

美联储及其全球同行正面临着货币政策的抉择困境。如果过快放宽货币条件，他们可能会让通胀预期在公众意识中根深蒂固。相反，维持高利率时间过长，则有可能将脆弱的经济推入彻底的衰退，扼杀企业的投资和招聘。

地缘政治格局使这一高风险的平衡举措更加复杂。关键海运通道的航运中断已将货运费率推高至大流行病时期以来未见的高位，而中东的地缘政治紧张局势也给全球石油供应蒙上了一层挥之不去的阴影。这些供给侧冲击在很大程度上对提高利率这一粗放工具“免疫”，从而使货币当局处于不稳固的尴尬境地。

对于新加坡这样高度开放、依赖贸易的经济体而言，这些全球逆流显得尤为严峻。新加坡金融管理局必须不断调整其基于汇率的货币政策，以保护国内消费者免受进口通胀的影响，同时避免严重削弱出口竞争力。这是一次微妙的经济“走钢丝”，几乎不容许任何政策失误。

归根结底，通胀的卷土重来是一个令人清醒的警示：大流行病后的经济转型远未完成。结构性转变，包括代价高昂的绿色能源转型和全球供应链重组，都表明超低通胀和极低利率的时代可能已一去不返。企业和消费者都必须做好准备，迎接宏观经济长期波动的新常态。

gems.s: It is a delicate economic tightrope walk that leaves little room for policy missteps.
gems.why: This sentence uses the metaphor of a tightrope walk to vividly convey the immense difficulty and high risk involved in economic policymaking. 在英文写作中，使用“走钢丝”的比喻能够生动形象地向读者传达经济政策制定过程中的极高难度和巨大风险。
